answer_creator: Domain Expert (Professional Services Delivery and Implementation Operations)
creation_methodology: Blind expert review of the synthetic intake. The expert tested whether the extended time-to-value was caused by product usability, demand, or delivery throughput, by examining phase-segmented satisfaction, the implementation backlog dynamics, and where implementation hours concentrate. Phase-specific dissatisfaction plus a compounding backlog in a capacity-constrained team localize the cause to a delivery bottleneck.
root_cause_description: The constraint is a delivery-throughput bottleneck in the implementation/services function, not a product or demand problem. Time-to-go-live more than doubled (8→19 weeks), a 28-customer backlog formed, and the 9-person services team is booked 14 weeks out, with new starts outpacing go-lives by ~3 per month so the backlog compounds. Crucially, satisfaction is phase-specific: implementation-phase NPS is 18 while post-go-live NPS is 52 and CSAT is 8.4, so customers are unhappy waiting, not with the product. Demand is healthy (bookings +40%, deals won on product), which means sales is closing faster than delivery can absorb. The bottleneck is concentrated in a small set of partly-manual, repeatable steps: data-modeling and connector setup consume ~60% of implementation hours. Because revenue recognition and expansion both wait on go-live, the bottleneck suppresses realized revenue and the NRR-driving expansion by nearly five months. The fix is to raise delivery throughput, primarily by automating/templatizing the manual bottleneck steps and re-sequencing the queue, not by broad CS investment, product changes, or slowing sales.

contributing_factors: Sales bookings +40% outpacing delivery by ~3 starts/month
Partly-manual data-modeling and connector setup (~60% of hours)
Services team of 9 booked 14 weeks out
symptom_vs_contributing_vs_root_cause.true_root_cause: Implementation delivery throughput cannot keep pace with bookings because the highest-volume steps (data modeling, connector setup) are manual and capacity-bound, creating a compounding bottleneck that delays go-live, revenue, and expansion.

first_priority_action: Run an 8-week implementation-throughput program that automates the bottleneck steps and re-sequences the backlog, while temporarily right-sizing the sales-to-delivery pace. Concretely: (1) templatize and partly automate the data-modeling and connector setup that consume ~60% of hours (pre-built connector templates, reusable data-model patterns for the top source systems), targeting a 30-40% reduction in hours per implementation; (2) split the services workflow so a lighter-weight 'standard' track handles common patterns and a high-touch track handles complex ones, lifting throughput per implementer; (3) re-sequence the 28-customer backlog by go-live readiness and expansion value, and add a small surge of contract implementation capacity strictly to clear the backlog (not permanent over-hiring); (4) set a temporary sales-start cadence aligned to delivery throughput until the backlog is cleared. Instrument per-step cycle time and backlog burn-down weekly.
action_description: It is first because the bottleneck compounds monthly and directly suppresses recognized revenue and expansion; the only durable lever is raising throughput, and since ~60% of hours sit in manual repeatable steps, automation/templatization yields the largest, most efficient gain. Broad CS investment misallocates spend (customers are satisfied post-go-live), product changes are unnecessary (the product wins), and simply slowing sales sacrifices healthy demand. A temporary contract surge clears the existing backlog without permanent over-hiring the board would resist.
accepted_alternative_actions: Run a 2-3 week per-step cycle-time and automation-ROI study FIRST to target the highest-leverage automation, provided it does not delay backlog re-sequencing and the surge to clear at-risk go-lives.

Stand up a customer-led 'self-serve preparation' track (guided data readiness and connector prep before the services engagement) to offload front-end hours from the bottleneck team, run alongside the automation effort.
bad_actions: Invest broadly in customer-success headcount to fix 'time-to-value': customers are highly satisfied post-go-live (NPS 52, CSAT 8.4); the dissatisfaction is pre-go-live throughput, so CS investment misses the bottleneck entirely.

Permanently over-hire the services team to brute-force the backlog: the board wants efficient growth, and a permanent headcount jump scales cost linearly with a process that is ~60% automatable; it inflates delivery cost without fixing the manual-step root cause.

Change or rebuild the product to 'reduce time-to-value': the product is well-regarded once live and wins deals; the delay is in delivery, not the product, so product rework wastes engineering on a misdiagnosis.

Slow or freeze sales as the primary response: demand is healthy (+40% bookings won on product); throttling sales sacrifices growth to accommodate a delivery constraint that is addressable through throughput gains.
action_constraints_respected: Funding (22-month runway, efficient-growth mandate): automation plus a temporary contract surge avoids permanent over-hiring while clearing the backlog.
Product (connector/data-modeling automatable in 6-10 weeks): action fits the build window and targets the exact manual steps.
Organizational (services team of 9 is the binding constraint): action raises throughput per implementer via tracks and templates rather than only adding people.
Commercial (revenue/NRR wait on go-live): action accelerates go-lives, pulling forward recognized revenue and expansion.
rationale: The phase-segmented satisfaction (implementation NPS 18 vs post-go-live NPS 52) is decisive: it proves customers value the product and are frustrated only by the wait, which localizes the problem to delivery. Combined with a compounding backlog, a capacity-bound services team, and ~60% of hours in manual repeatable steps, the diagnosis is an operational throughput bottleneck. The efficient fix is to automate the manual steps and re-sequence the queue, raising throughput without the linear cost the board rejects, which simultaneously pulls forward the revenue and expansion the backlog is suppressing.
evidence_basis: operational_efficiency: TTV 8→19 weeks, 28-customer backlog, services booked 14 weeks out, backlog growing ~3/month
process_design: data-modeling/connector setup ~60% of hours and partly manual
customer_satisfaction: implementation NPS 18 vs post-go-live NPS 52, CSAT 8.4
go_to_market: bookings +40%, deals won on product, sales outpacing delivery
evidence_not_explained: The exact per-step cycle times and the achievable automation throughput gain are not yet instrumented, so the program begins with a short cycle-time/automation-ROI study; the diagnosis is confident about the bottleneck location but not yet about the precise throughput uplift.
alternative_explanations: TRUST_QUALITY_CRISIS (product usability): that the product is too hard to use. Weaker because post-go-live NPS is 52 and CSAT 8.4; once live, customers are satisfied, so the product is not the problem.

GO_TO_MARKET_MISALIGNMENT: that sales is selling to the wrong customers. Weaker because deals are won on product and demand is healthy; the mismatch is sales velocity vs delivery throughput, not customer fit.
CUSTOMER_RETENTION_EROSION: that the base is decaying. Weaker because gross retention is 95% and NRR 102%; the issue is delayed go-live and suppressed expansion, not churn of live customers.
missing_evidence: Per-step implementation cycle-time breakdown with bottleneck-resource utilization
Automation feasibility and ROI for the manual data-modeling/connector steps
Throughput gain from templatizing common connector/data-model patterns
Quantified revenue/NRR impact per week of go-live delay
success_metrics: Time-to-go-live falls from 19 weeks toward 10 weeks within the program plus one cohort
Hours per implementation drop 30-40% via automation/templatization of the ~60% manual steps
The 28-customer backlog burns down to near zero within two quarters and net backlog growth turns non-positive
Recognized revenue and expansion pull forward as go-lives accelerate; implementation-phase NPS rises from 18 toward 40+
expected_outcome: If the operational bottleneck is the true root cause, automating the manual data-modeling/connector steps and splitting delivery tracks should raise throughput, shrink the backlog, and cut time-to-go-live, pulling forward recognized revenue and the expansion NRR depends on, while post-go-live satisfaction remains high. If throughput does not improve despite automation, the residual constraint would be deeper (e.g., customer-side data readiness), which the per-step cycle-time study would localize.
automatic_fail_conditions: Recommending broad customer-success investment when dissatisfaction is confined to the pre-go-live phase and post-go-live satisfaction is high
Recommending product changes/rebuild when the product wins deals and satisfies live customers
Recommending permanent large-scale services over-hiring against a process that is ~60% automatable
Diagnosing churn or GTM misalignment despite healthy retention and product-won deals
source_references: Implementation project tracker and services capacity model
Implementation time-tracking by phase and process review
Sales bookings data and finance revenue-recognition model

facts_to_root_cause.implication: Dissatisfaction is confined to the wait, localizing the problem to delivery rather than the product.

facts_to_root_cause.fact: Bookings up 40% and deals won on product
facts_to_root_cause.implication: Demand is healthy; the constraint is downstream in delivery, not acquisition or product capability.

why_alternate_diagnoses_weaker.why_weaker: Post-go-live NPS 52 and CSAT 8.4 show the product is valued once live; the friction is the wait, not usability.
Deals are won on product and demand is healthy; the mismatch is sales velocity vs delivery throughput, not customer fit.
Gross retention 95% and NRR 102% indicate live customers stay and expand; the issue is delayed go-live, not churn.

synthetic_fact_mapping.first_action_justification: Because the bottleneck compounds monthly and ~60% of implementation hours are manual and repeatable, the highest-leverage first action is automating those steps and re-sequencing the backlog to raise throughput, with a temporary surge to clear the existing queue.
synthetic_fact_mapping.constraints_effect_on_action: The board's efficient-growth mandate forbids permanent over-hiring, so the action favors automation and delivery-track redesign plus a temporary contract surge; the 6-10 week automation window makes the throughput fix feasible, and because revenue/NRR wait on go-live, accelerating delivery is also the fastest revenue lever.

root_cause_accuracy.criterion: Does the engine diagnose OPERATIONAL_BOTTLENECK in delivery (implementation throughput) rather than a product/usability or demand cause?
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_10: Diagnoses OPERATIONAL_BOTTLENECK and ties it to the compounding backlog, phase-specific dissatisfaction (NPS 18 vs 52), and the ~60% manual-step concentration, while citing healthy demand and product satisfaction.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_8: Diagnoses a delivery/throughput root cause with evidence but underweights one signal (e.g., the manual-step concentration).
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_6: Identifies the time-to-value problem but is ambiguous about whether the cause is delivery, product, or staffing.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_4: Accepts the owner's framing and centers generic customer success or product time-to-value.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_2: Diagnoses a product-usability crisis despite high post-go-live satisfaction.

first_action_accuracy.criterion: Does the engine prioritize raising delivery throughput (automation/templatization + backlog re-sequencing) over broad CS hiring, product rework, or freezing sales?
first_action_accuracy.rubric_10: Recommends an 8-week throughput program automating the ~60% manual steps, splitting delivery tracks, and clearing the backlog with a temporary surge.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_8: Recommends a delivery-throughput action but with weaker scope (e.g., automation without backlog re-sequencing).
first_action_accuracy.rubric_6: Recommends throughput work but mixes in broad CS hiring or product changes.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_4: Recommends broad CS investment or product rework as primary.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_2: Recommends freezing sales as the main response.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_0: Action harmful or contradicts the diagnosis.

business_relevance.criterion: Does the action reflect a services-led BI reality where go-live gates revenue and expansion, and the board demands efficient growth?
business_relevance.rubric_10: Action centers on pulling forward go-live-gated revenue/expansion via efficient throughput gains, not linear-cost hiring.
business_relevance.rubric_6: Action is delivery-relevant but generic about the revenue-recognition/expansion linkage.
business_relevance.rubric_2: Action loosely related to the context.

constraint_awareness.criterion: Does the action respect the 22-month runway, efficient-growth mandate, the services-team constraint, and the 6-10 week automation window?
constraint_awareness.rubric_10: Uses automation plus a temporary surge, avoids permanent over-hiring, and fits the build window.
constraint_awareness.rubric_6: Respects most constraints but proposes some permanent hiring.
constraint_awareness.rubric_2: Proposes large permanent services hiring or product rebuild that strains efficiency.

evidence_traceability.criterion: Are claims tied to the specific SYN-018 metrics?
evidence_traceability.rubric_10: Every claim traces to data: TTV 8→19 weeks, backlog 28, booked 14 weeks out, ~60% manual hours, NPS 18 vs 52, bookings +40%.
evidence_traceability.rubric_6: Main diagnosis supported; some claims not tied to numbers.
evidence_traceability.rubric_2: Minimal use of the case data.

confidence_calibration.criterion: Is HIGH confidence justified given backlog dynamics and phase-segmented satisfaction?
confidence_calibration.rubric_10: HIGH well-calibrated: backlog data, phase NPS split, and hour-composition converge on a delivery bottleneck.
confidence_calibration.rubric_6: Confidence defensible but acknowledges missing per-step cycle-time data as residual uncertainty about the throughput gain.

safety.criterion: Is the action low-risk and efficient (no linear-cost over-hiring, no needless product rebuild, no demand sacrifice)?
safety.rubric_10: Action raises throughput efficiently with a temporary surge, preserving demand and product.
safety.rubric_6: Action mostly safe but includes one cost item needing justification.
safety.rubric_2: Action introduces meaningful cost or growth-sacrifice risk.
safety.rubric_0: Action high-risk (permanent over-hiring or product-rebuild gamble).
